runs.text: turbandoſe como diante de algũa peſſoa de reſ-

lines.note: This continues f165's `Faimǒ`: becoming confused before a respected person. `reſ-` belongs to `reſpeito` below, not the next Japanese example.
`Faimǒ tçucamatçutta` is a deferential statement of having become confused or forgetful. The polite verb helps explain the socially intimidating context.
`Fainobori` combines crawling or clinging with ascending. Portuguese describes climbing while holding on rather than ordinary walking uphill.

runs.text: as mãos, como quem ſobe a algũ lugar ingreme

lines.note: The climber uses the hands to ascend a steep place. This supplies the physical manner implicit in the Japanese compound.
A fortress is one example of the steep place. `Item` switches from a person to a creeping plant.

runs.text: ſubir da era por algũa aruore, ou parede, &c.

lines.note: Ivy climbing a tree or wall is the botanical extension of `Fainobori`. Here Portuguese `era` means ivy.
`Faino zǒ`, 肺の臓, means lungs; `Bofes` confirms the organ. This repeats the anatomical expression encountered on f165.
`Faiqen` 拝見 is explained by reverently seeing; the Portuguese example concerns reading a letter, not eyesight alone.
`Gojǒuo faiqen tçucama-` begins a deferential acknowledgment of the recipient's letter. The polite verb is completed below.

runs.text: Vi, ou li a carta de voſſa mercè.

lines.note: `Vi, ou li` means “I saw or read your letter.” The initial word is Portuguese `Vi`, not the Latin example marker `Vt`; the scan supports that contextual distinction.
`Faiqiacu` concerns discarding or destroying, compatible with 廃却. `Sutaruru` and the Portuguese destructive verbs distinguish it from respectful 拝 compounds.
`Faiqiacu ſuru` makes the noun into a verb. The example marker introduces only that construction, with no additional Portuguese definition on this line.
`Vôrai ſuru coto` explains going about, compatible with 徘徊. `Correr terras` means traveling through lands, not necessarily running physically.

runs.text: ou andar peregrinando por diuerſas partes.

lines.note: Portuguese adds wandering or journeying through different places. This confirms the movement sense rather than an honorific reading of `Fai-`.
`Cuniguniuo faiquai itaſu` is traveling through various countries. Here `Diſcorrer` means ranging or passing through, not simply discussing a topic.
The object is several kingdoms or countries. This completes the travel example from the preceding line.

runs.text: Fairan. i, Vogami, miru. i, Faiqen.

lines.note: `Fairan` 拝覧 is equated with `Vogami, miru` and `Faiqen`. Both reading and seeing can realize respectful inspection.
“Or see with reverence” completes the gloss. The distinction from ordinary looking is social register, not a different visual action.
`Tamauaru` identifies humble receiving, supporting 拝領. `riǒzuru` should be understood within that compound rather than as an unrelated word.

runs.text: ceber algũa couſa de peſſoa nobre. Vt,

lines.note: The item is received from a noble person. `Ca-` begins the Japanese sword example, not a Portuguese word.
`Ca- / tanauo fairiǒ ſuru` means receiving a sword respectfully. The second `Catana` is embedded in the Portuguese translation.
The donor is a lord or noble person. This completes the direction and social status of the gift in the preceding example.
`Fairi, u, itta` is the entering verb はいる. Its short Portuguese gloss distinguishes it from the adjacent compounds in 拝.
`Xebai iuori` is a narrow dwelling or hut. The headword's precise historical formation should not be inferred merely from modern はいる; `P.` is an editorial label.
The Portuguese specifies a hut that is narrow and small. It supplies the dwelling sense needed to interpret the previous Japanese phrase.
`Fairiu` is glossed as a stratagem or contrivance. Earlier NINJAL comparison recorded the same spelling with a likely intended `Fairiǔ`; that length restoration remains annotation, not transcription.
`Faisǔ` describes reverential or diligent attendance. The printed `vaxiru` is suspicious if one expects はしる in 拝趨; keep the discrepancy visible rather than treating the automatic kana as proof.
Serving with diligence and respect completes the definition. This supports the honorific action but does not independently settle the unusual Japanese letter above.
`Faitaca` ハイタカ is a hawk that catches quail. The prey named in Portuguese helps distinguish it from an unspecified bird.
`Faitçuqi` is clinging while climbing. The Portuguese comparison begins here and names ivy below.
Ivy adhering to a tree supplies the model for the preceding verb. The gloss concerns attachment as well as upward movement.
`Vogami ſaſaguru` explains respectful presentation. Portuguese associates `Faitei` with a deferential response, so the following epistolary usage matters.

runs.text: peſſoa alta cõ reuerencia: palaura q̃ ſe põe nos

lines.note: The addressee is high-ranking. The word is used in written addresses or superscriptions, not merely spoken as a reply.

runs.text: ſobreſcritos das cartas, ou Vias que vão em

lines.note: Letters and `Vias` are mentioned as vehicles of the response. The latter's interpretation is not secure enough here to label it automatically as Japanese vocabulary.
These communications answer honored people. The line closes the description of the term's placement in correspondence.
`Cubari, atçuru` means distributing or allotting, supporting 配当. This noun differs from the identically spelled respectful-reply entry below.

runs.text: Repoſta com reuerencia a peſſoa nobre.

lines.note: This `Faitǒ` denotes a reverent answer to a noble person, compatible with 拝答. The homograph above instead concerns allocation.
`Sacazzuqi` gives サカヅキ, identifying the cup sense. `S.` is an editorial label; the unusual printed headword spacing is not resolved by its meaning.
`Faiuatari` describes spreading or passing from one place to another. The compound combines creeping with crossing.

runs.text: hũa parte a outra como era, ou erua de latada q̃

lines.note: Ivy or a trellised plant provides the first example. The movement is between supports, completed below.

runs.text: paſſa de hũ pao a outro. Itẽ, Eſtẽderſe o bicho,

lines.note: The plant passes from one stick to another. `Item` begins the same extension or bridging movement in an animal.

runs.text: ou cobra, & paſſar de hũ ramo a outro, &c.

lines.note: A creature or snake stretches from branch to branch. This completes the animal example of the preceding creeping-across verb.

runs.text: Repoſta que ſe daa com reuerencia:

lines.note: `Faiuô` is a reverential reply, distinct from crawling compounds. The following lines explain its written epistolary setting.

runs.text: palaura que ſe poem nos ſobreſcritos das car-

lines.note: The expression is placed in the superscription of letters. Read `car-` with the next line rather than treating it as Japanese.

runs.text: tas que vão pera peſſoas honradas.

lines.note: The letters go to honored people. This closes the usage restriction rather than adding another sense of the headword.
`Sutareta iye`, an abandoned house, explains 廃屋. Portuguese gives a fallen or old house, a compatible but not identical descriptive emphasis.
This `Faixi, ſuru, ita` means worshipping, from 拝. The next column begins another verb of the same spelling with a different meaning.
This `Faixi` instead means casting away or exiling. Keep it separate from the worshipping verb at the preceding column's foot.
`Qimiuo yentǒye` sends the lord to a distant island. The honorific verb continues across the physical line break.

runs.text: Deſterrãdo a o ſenhor pera hũa ilha

lines.note: `faixitatema- / tçurite` completes the deferential exile construction. Portuguese confirms exiling the lord to an island; the final adjective follows below.
`longe` completes “a distant island.” This short line supplies distance, not another headword or geographical name.

runs.text: Offerecer algũa couſa ao ſenhor, ou

lines.note: `Faixin` denotes offering something to a lord. The recipient rather than the object determines the honorific interpretation.
A noble person is the alternative recipient. This finishes the offering definition without a separate Japanese example.

runs.text: Faixo. Sutçuru tocoro. i, Runinno toco-

lines.note: `Sutçuru tocoro` and `Runinno toco-` explain an exile destination. `Runin` is a banished person, not a modern masterless-samurai gloss imposed here.
`toco- / ro` completes “place.” Portuguese `Lugar de deſterro` confirms a place of banishment.
`Vogami, vquru` describes respectfully receiving someone, in a deferential reception context. Avoid choosing kanji solely from the mechanical reading.
The reception occurs in one's house and is reverent. This is hosting a person, not receiving a gift as in 拝領.
`Faixo, i, faijo` names a shrine or small oratory. The memorial context in the next lines distinguishes this from the exile homograph.

runs.text: aleuanta pera algum defunto pondolhe ſeu no-

lines.note: The oratory is erected for a deceased person. Their name is placed on an object specified below.
The name is written on a board. The displaced `( ruina.` physically shares this row but logically completes the next entry's Portuguese definition.
`Sutare, yabururu` explains destruction or ruin, compatible with 敗壊. Read the Portuguese together with the displaced `ruina` above, without changing physical line order.
`Faiyet` corresponds to 拝閲, reverential inspection; final `-t` is a historical checked ending. `qemiſuru` is the reading/examining gloss, not an accidental word ending.
`reue- / rencia` completes “with reverence.” The line supplies the manner of inspection defined above.
`Faiyoxe` begins the gathering of cremation ashes. Relatives and friends, rather than officials, are the actors named here.

runs.text: do morto ao outro dia no campo as cinzas do

lines.note: They gather the next day at the cremation place. The ashes belong to the deceased body described in the next line.
The burned body's ashes are collected and buried. `Faiyo-` begins the corresponding Japanese verbal example.
`Faiyo- / xe ſuru` means performing the ash-gathering; `Faiyoxeni mairu` means going to it. The Portuguese translation continues below.
“Collect and bury these ashes” completes the example. This confirms that the action is funerary, not ordinary sweeping.
`Faji, l, fajino qi` gives a tree name and its expanded form. The Portuguese identifies a practical use rather than a botanical description.
The wood supplies eating sticks, or chopsticks. This connects the tree entry with the similar account on f165 without merging their spellings.
`Fajicami` is はじかみ, here glossed as ginger. The faint Portuguese word deserves glyph-level caution; its botanical sense is clearer than each printed letter.
`Fajimari` means a beginning. It is the noun, distinguished from the inflected verb in the next entry.
`Fajimari, u, atta` is the intransitive “begin.” The Portuguese reflexive form similarly presents something beginning, not someone initiating an object.
`Fajime` is another nominal beginning or commencement. The following entry supplies its verbal use.
`Fajime, uru, eta` means beginning something. Portuguese explicitly says it combines with many verb stems, introducing examples below.
`Yomifajimuru` is beginning to read, with 読み as the preceding stem. This illustrates the compounding rule rather than a separate headword.

The first gloss finishes “begin to read.” The fresh pass and a larger crop support `Caqifajimuru`, beginning to write: `Caqi-` is the writing stem, parallel to `Yomi-` above, not the earlier `Caqu-` reading.
`Come- / çar a eſcreuer` completes “begin to write.” This confirms the intended sense of the questionable Japanese compound above.
`Fajimete` means “for the first time.” The example begins here and must be interpreted with the respectful meeting expression below.
`Fajimete vǒ meni cacaru` means meeting someone for the first time. The Portuguese translation continues with the object of seeing.
`que vos vejo` completes “this is the first time I see you.” The direct Portuguese wording translates a deferential Japanese expression.
`Fajimeto xite` is explained as “principally,” not merely “at the beginning.” `Adu.` identifies adverbial use.
`Coreuo fajimeto xite` means taking this especially or foremost. The Portuguese “this principally” supports that selective emphasis.
`Fajiqi` is flicking with the fingers. The displayed paradigm's `ijta` is unusual beside expected `ita`; retain the printed sequence rather than inferring an inflectional correction.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Dar couces o animal, principalmen

lines.note: An additional sense is an animal kicking. The restriction `principalmen` continues onto the next line.

runs.text: te boi, ou vaca; ¶ Item, Largar algum

lines.note: Oxen and cows are the principal animals meant. `Item` then begins releasing something held under tension.

runs.text: pao, ou ramo da aruore que eſta enteſado, ou

lines.note: A piece of wood or branch has been bent or tensioned. Releasing it creates the springing motion underlying this sense of はじく.
A rod is another example of the tensioned object. The comparison `abuis` is not securely identified here and should not be translated as a known Japanese term without evidence.

runs.text: Portas abertas do meo para cima co-

lines.note: `Fajitomi` denotes doors or shutters opening from the middle upward, compatible with 半蔀. The physical description continues with their grating-like form.
“Like gratings” completes the shutter definition. This describes construction rather than an additional opening action.
`Fama` is 浜, a beach. The next homographs have specialized object senses rather than geography.

runs.text: Pedras que ſe tomão ao contrario ven-

lines.note: This `Fama` denotes stones captured from an opponent. The game is identified in the following line.

runs.text: cendo no jogo do Go de Iapão.

lines.note: `Go` is the Japanese board game. The definition concerns captured stones, compatible with the go term ハマ, not pebbles gathered at a beach.

runs.text: Hum circulo de palha, ou de junco que

lines.note: Another `Fama` is a straw or rush ring. Its users and activity continue on f167, so the object should not be identified from its shape alone.
